name: pesarattu
instructions:
From Priya Krishna's Indian-ish. A South Indian (Andhra) crepe made from soaked whole green mung beans blended with ginger and serrano into a smooth batter, then fried into thin dosa-like crepes on a hot pan. Topped with finely diced raw red onion.

See notes for a real technique caveat — getting proper dosa-like crepes is hard without a nonstick pan (see NONSTICK PAN + PROTEIN FILM note) — and for an experimental want-to-try: food-processor-and-bake-as-quesadilla method to bypass the stickiness.

SERVES 4 (~8 crepes).

=== INGREDIENTS ===

- 1 cup whole green MUNG BEANS (or BROWN LENTILS — see BROWN LENTILS WORK FINE note), soaked at least 4 hours (overnight preferred)
- 1 inch fresh ginger, peeled
- 1 SERRANO chile (NON-OPTIONAL — see SERRANO note)
- ~1/3 to 1/2 cup water (enough to blend into a smooth pourable batter)
- ~3/4 tsp salt
- ghee or neutral oil for the pan
- 1 red onion, finely diced (raw, for topping)

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. SOAK the mung beans (or brown lentils) in plenty of cool water for at least 4 hours, overnight preferred. Drain.

2. BLEND: add the drained beans, ginger, serrano, water, and salt to a blender. Blend until smooth — the batter should be pourable pancake-batter consistency, no chunks. Add water gradually; more is easier than less to fix.

3. HEAT A NONSTICK PAN (see notes — nonstick is really important here) over medium heat with a small amount of ghee or oil.

4. POUR ~1/4 CUP BATTER into the pan and immediately SPREAD THIN using the back of a spoon or the bottom of a ladle in circular motions, dosa-style. Thin crepe is the target.

5. COOK ~2-3 min until the edges lift and the surface looks set/dry. Flip and cook 1 min more.

6. SERVE topped generously with finely diced raw red onion. Traditional accompaniment is a chutney (coconut chutney or ginger chutney) but the onion alone is enough.
notes:
From Priya Krishna's Indian-ish cookbook. Andhra-style pesarattu — the whole-mung-bean crepe that's a distinct South Indian dish from the more common lentil dosas.

=== BROWN LENTILS WORK JUST AS WELL AS MUNG BEANS ===

Whole green mung beans are the traditional and canonical choice. In practice BROWN LENTILS work just as well — same soaking, same blend, same behavior in the pan. If mung beans aren't on hand, don't sweat it; brown lentils are a genuine substitute (not a compromise). Both belong in the ingredient list.

=== NONSTICK PAN + PROTEIN FILM — LOAD-BEARING TECHNIQUE CAVEAT ===

Getting proper dosa-like crepes out of this batter is REALLY HARD WITHOUT A NONSTICK PAN. The reason is a protein-film effect: the mung bean (or lentil) protein forms a sticky film against the hot pan surface. On a NONSTICK pan, that film is exactly what makes the crepe hold together and lift cleanly — it's what makes dosas work. On a CAST IRON or STAINLESS pan, that same protein film becomes an aggressive sticking layer — the crepe rips apart when you try to flip it, and you spend the rest of the meal scraping baked-on lentil paste off the pan.

Use nonstick. Cast iron is not the pan for this dish.

=== FRYING THE MUSH WHOLE (NOT AS CREPES) — TASTES DELICIOUS BUT STICKS ===

If you skip the spreading step and just fry a scoop of the batter as a thicker cake (like a pancake or a large fritter), it TASTES DELICIOUS — same batter, same flavor, just a different shape. But the protein-film sticking problem is even worse in this format: without spreading thin, the batter has more contact with the pan and more time to bond as it thickens through. You'll end up with a burnt sticky bottom and a mess of stuck-on mung mush.

Both formats want nonstick. If you don't have nonstick, wait until you do — there's no clean workaround with a regular pan.

=== WANT TO TRY — FOOD PROCESSOR (NO WATER) + BAKE AS QUESADILLA IN THE OVEN ===

An experimental direction to bypass the sticky-protein problem entirely:

- Make the batter in a FOOD PROCESSOR instead of a blender, without adding water. The food processor can pulverize the soaked beans without needing liquid — you'd end up with a thick paste rather than a pourable batter.
- Spread the thick paste between two tortillas (like a QUESADILLA) and BAKE it in the oven instead of frying on a stovetop pan.
- The oven bake would cook the mung paste through without the pan-contact sticking, and the tortillas would carry the structure so the paste doesn't need to hold itself together.

Untested. If it works, it would let you make pesarattu-flavored quesadillas even without a nonstick pan.

=== SERRANO IS NON-OPTIONAL — BUT BE CAREFUL ABOUT SPICE LOAD ===

The serrano isn't a garnish or an optional heat — it's a load-bearing flavor ingredient in the batter. The green-chile vegetal-heat character defines pesarattu; without it, the crepe tastes flat and bean-forward-only.

BUT SERRANOS ARE HOT — be careful with the quantity. START WITH HALF A SERRANO for a full 1-cup batch and taste (blend, then taste a spoonful before cooking). Add more if it needs it; hard to walk back if you overshoot. A single whole serrano can easily push a modest batch into aggressive-heat territory.

Jalapeño can substitute if serrano isn't available (see [[mint-cilantro-skillet]]'s serrano-vs-jalapeño note for the parallel case), but dice smaller and adjust for the difference in heat — jalapeño is milder, so you can use more.

=== RAW RED ONION TOPPING IS PART OF THE DISH ===

Priya's recipe (and traditional pesarattu) tops the crepe with finely diced raw red onion at serving. This isn't just a garnish — the raw sharp onion + the earthy-warm crepe is the whole flavor architecture. Don't skip it. Dice small so the onion distributes evenly per bite.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- [[coconut-mung-bean-curry]]: the other mung-bean recipe in the cookbook. Same base ingredient, entirely different preparation (curry with coconut milk, not crepe).
- [[mint-cilantro-skillet]]: shares the serrano-as-fresh-chile approach (see SERRANO note above).
